facts.text: The Elwha River runs from the Olympic Mountains of Washington State, much of it inside Olympic National Park, to the Strait of Juan de Fuca.
Before the dams, all five species of Pacific salmon, along with steelhead and other sea-run fish, returned to the Elwha to spawn.
Work on the Elwha Dam began in 1910; it started producing power in 1913, supplying a pulp mill in the town of Port Angeles.
A second, taller dam, Glines Canyon Dam, began operating in 1927 eight miles upstream of the Elwha Dam.
The Elwha Dam was about 32 meters high and the Glines Canyon Dam about 64 meters high.
A Washington State law of 1890 required dams to let fish pass, but the builder ignored it, and both dams were built without any way for fish to get past.
The dams left salmon returning from the sea with only about five miles of river below the Elwha Dam.
The dams also trapped sediment behind them, so riverbanks and spawning beds downstream wore away, and the shoreline at the river mouth eroded quickly.
In 1992 the U.S. Congress passed a law aimed at fully restoring the river and its native fish and allowing the dams to be removed.
Before the dams came down, two water treatment facilities costing $79 million were built between 2008 and 2010 to protect the water supply of Port Angeles from the trapped sediment.
The largest dam removal in U.S. history began in September 2011; the Elwha Dam was gone about six months later, and the Glines Canyon Dam was removed by 2014.
Removing the dams reopened more than 70 miles of river and stream habitat to salmon.
Within months of the dams' removal, salmon were spawning inside the national park for the first time in 100 years.
About 19 million cubic meters of sediment had built up behind the dams, and its release was described as the largest controlled release of sediment into a river and the sea in history.
While removal was under way, heavy loads of mud in the water sharply cut the number and variety of small river animals below the dams, though many recovered quickly.
The released sediment and wood at first disturbed salmon, but once the sediment settled, river sections improved and gained gravel for spawning.
Summer steelhead, once thought lost from the Elwha, have come back, and steelhead have recovered faster than Chinook salmon.
Years after removal, the productivity of adult Chinook salmon was still below target, and full recovery is expected to take decades.
According to the U.S. Geological Survey, the two reservoirs did not reduce flooding in the river valley.
